attachment.cliPrefix: You are Claude Code, Anthropic's official CLI for Claude, running within the Claude Agent SDK.

content.content:
1	# The report and the record
2	
3	## What every report holds
4	
5	Your brief says where your report goes: a file that it names, your final message, or both. If it names no file, your report is your final message.
6	
7	A finding is something that your work learned about the tree or the language, and that the record does not hold yet. Examples: a defect, a behaviour that departs from the specification or from a decision of the curator, a measurement. What you did along the way is not a finding, for example the files that you read or edited. Your transcript keeps that.
8	
9	A fact is a finding that is an established property of the tree, the language, the library or their tools, and that later work builds on. A defect also gets its ledger row, and a fact about it may cite the row.
10	
11	A point to report is a kind of change or finding that the curator wants to review. Your brief names its points to report. Examples: a changed line of a test that the team wrote, a checker edit inside a change to the library, a changed line of the model program.
12	
13	Put each of these that you have in your report, in this form, whatever else your brief asks for:
14	
15	- **Defects.** Each defect that you measured, and the test or ledger row that records it (`tests-writing.md`, "How a defect is recorded").
16	- **Sentences of the specification made false.** Each sentence of the specification that your change makes false, quoted with its file and line. Such a sentence says what walk or the compiled path does. It is in the effect of an Appendix I entry (`Specification/appendices/changes.tex`), or in a `\revision` or `\note{}` box beside a passage.
17	- **Decisions.** Each choice that you made among alternatives, as a decision apart from the findings: what you chose, the alternatives, and the evidence, cited. If no decision of the curator covers it, say so, and say which reading you acted on. A decision left as a line inside the findings counts as not made.
18	- **Points to report.** Each point that your brief names and the work reached, with its evidence, also one that only part of the work reached.
19	- **For FACTS.** Each fact that your work established, in the hand-over form of "Writing to the record". If your brief let you write FACTS, give instead the number of each entry that you added or rewrote. If your work established no fact, write "none".
20	- **Commands.** Each command that you had to work out because this skill does not give it, with what it does.
21	- **Questions for the curator.** If something needs the curator's decision, list it as a decision not taken, in the form that `exploring.md` gives. The reader of your report brings it to the curator. Do not choose which of your items anyone reviews.
22	
23	## At a point to report
24	
25	- If the work reaches a point to report, do what the brief says for it. For example, a brief can say that a defect in the code is recorded in a ledger row and not repaired.
26	- Then finish the work.
27	- If a step cannot be undone, or would change a decision of the curator, report it instead. List it as a decision not taken, with its alternatives.
28	
29	## Timings and citations
30	
31	- If you take a timing that you will keep, run nothing else beside it. All agents of the session share the machine's cores (the `cloud-container` skill).
32	- Name the machine with every timing: `nproc`, the CPU's model and MHz, the load at start, the JDK, `FORTRESS_THREADS`. Only a pair of timings taken in one run measures a difference.
33	- If you take a measurement again because the code changed, say what changed.
34	- In a report, cite the tree at file:line, and quote results, two to five lines, each with its command. Never cite a file under `tmp/`.
35	
36	## POSITIONS and FACTS
37	
38	POSITIONS and FACTS describe the present: no dates, no names of who found what, no "corrected" or "superseded" notes. The history of each entry is in `POSITIONS-history.md` and `FACTS-history.md`, beside them. When your work needs the detail of an entry, print the report section that it cites (`$T 'doc:PATH#HEADING'`, below). Read its history only when the tree disagrees with the entry.
39	
40	Each entry is one line that starts with its permanent number: `F-87` in FACTS, `P-48` in POSITIONS. A FACTS entry is the fact as it stands now, what it means for the work, and the test that fails if the fact stops holding, under a bold title. If no test checks the fact, the entry gives the command and the output that show it. It points to the report section that holds the detail. Cite an entry by its number. If the reader must know what the entry says without printing it, add the first words of its title in quotes: F-87, "The first words ...".
41	
42	## The gap ledger
43	
44	The ledger's rows are the bug reports that the work fixes. A fix of a row starts with its reproduction, written as a test (`tests-writing.md`).
45	
46	A row is one line of eight cells, at most 1,200 characters, in the table of a topic section. Reports cite a row by its number, which it keeps for good. A new issue gets a new row.
47	
48	- Its status is one of seven words: `POSITIVE-VERIFIED`, `NEGATIVE-VERIFIED`, `NEGATIVE-BOUNDED`, `CONTESTED`, `RETIRED`, `FIXED`, `DUPLICATE`. The last three close a row. The row template (below) defines each.
49	- Its class is a kind and an area, such as `implementation gap (checker)`.
50	- The earlier text of a changed row is in `explorations/fortress-gap-ledger-history.md`.
51	
52	Read the ledger only through the queries below: it is too large to read whole.
53	
54	A row states its gap as it stands now. A note adds a fact. If your work changes what a row says, write the row's whole new line with `rewrite` (below), not a note that tells the repair.
55	
56	The heading reader of `ledger.py` does not expand the specification's `\Trait{X}` macro. So a row that names a library trait's section cites `Specification-1.0-frozen/` by line.
57	
58	## Reading the record
59	
60	Read only the slice of the record that you need. This tool prints whole entries, in parts of bounded size:
61	
62	    T=explorations/coordinator/tools/facts-extract.sh
63	
64	- `$T 'F-87'` prints one entry by its number, and `$T 'P-48'` one of POSITIONS. `$T 'F-87+'` adds each entry that F-87 cites by its number, and each entry that cites F-87. `$T 'history:F-87'` prints its history. Run one when your brief or a note cites an entry by its number.
65	- `$T 'positions:WORDS OF A TITLE'` prints one of the curator's decisions. Run it before you choose among ways to do something. If several titles hold the words, it names them.
66	- `$T 'WORDS OF A TITLE'` prints each FACTS entry whose bold title holds them, and `$T 'section:HEADING'` every entry of a FACTS section. Run one before you investigate a behaviour of the tree, and when your brief or a note names an entry. These queries and `positions:` read titles only: before you write that the record does not hold something, also grep FACTS and POSITIONS for its words.
67	- `$T 'index:WORDS'` prints the INDEX lines that hold the words. Run it to find the notes on a topic.
68	- `$T 'ledger-find:WORDS'` prints one line for each ledger row that holds every word. Run it when you meet a defect, before you investigate it.
69	- `$T 'ledger:ROW'` prints one row whole. Run it for each row that you need from a find, your brief or a note.
70	- `$T 'doc:PATH#HEADING'` prints a section of any note, or of a `.tex` chapter, and `$T 'map:FILE#HEADING'` a section of a note under `explorations/coordinator/map/`. Run one when your brief or a note names a section. `#HEADING@WORDS` prints only the table rows and list items of that section that hold every one of WORDS.
71	- `$T --check QUERY ...` prints only where each query matches and its size. Run it before a query whose size you do not know. `--part N` prints part N of a long output, and `--help` gives the rest.
72	
73	A word of a query that ends in `*` matches the start of a word. Any other word matches a whole word.
74	
75	Before you edit a file of the original tree, list the ledger rows that cite it, and read each row that your edit can change:
76	
77	    python3 explorations/coordinator/tools/ledger.py find --cites FILE
78	
79	## Writing to the record
80	
81	- Write FACTS and POSITIONS only with `explorations/coordinator/tools/record.py`, never by hand. `add` gives a new entry its number, and `set` rewrites an entry. The tool writes the entry to `FACTS.md` or `POSITIONS.md`, and its earlier text to the history file beside it. It commits nothing: commit both files in one commit. Its header gives its usage.
82	- If your brief lets you write FACTS, add each fact as a new entry in the section of its topic, in the commit that establishes it. Put its detail in a section of your report: the file:line citations, the commands with their output, and the measured numbers. Point the entry to that section, by your report's file and the section's heading. If your report is only your final message, hand the fact over instead. Spend no effort on the entry's wording: it is rewritten to the record's form after your work.
83	- If your brief does not let you write FACTS, hand each fact over in the "For FACTS" item of your report, with:
84	  - the fact as it stands now, in one sentence;
85	  - what it means for the work;
86	  - the number that a decision rests on, if any, with what it counts; if its parts belong to different ledger rows, the part of each row;
87	  - the test that fails if the fact stops holding, or the command and the output that show it;
88	  - the section of your report that holds the detail.
89	- If your brief lets you write FACTS, rewrite a wrong entry in place. Otherwise say in your hand-over that the entry is wrong, with the evidence.
90	- POSITIONS holds each of the curator's decisions, in one place. Everything else points there. Write a decision there only if your brief gives it to you to record. If you have evidence against one, do as `exploring.md` says.
91	- Put new files of the work under `explorations/`. If you add a note directly in `explorations/` or `explorations/reviews/`, add its line to INDEX: ``- `PATH`: `` and the first sentence of the note's header comment.
92	
93	Write the gap ledger only with `ledger.py`, which checks each line that it writes against the row template.
94	
95	    L="python3 explorations/coordinator/tools/ledger.py"
96	
97	To add a row:
98	
99	1. Print the row template, about 3 KB: `$T 'doc:explorations/fortress-gap-ledger.md#The row template'`.
100	2. Write the row as one line in a file under your tree's `tmp/`, with `?` in its number cell.
101	3. Run `$L add FILE --section TITLE`. It numbers the row and puts it in that section. If the row breaks the template, it adds nothing and prints each rule broken. `$L sections` lists the titles.
102	
103	To change a row:
104	
105	- `$L note N TEXT` adds TEXT to the notes of row N. It refuses a note that takes the row past 1,200 characters, or its notes cell past 700 characters. `$L note N TEXT --check` writes nothing. It says whether TEXT fits, and how many characters the notes and the row have left now and would have left with TEXT. These counts include the separator that the tool adds. It exits 0 if TEXT fits, and 1 if not. Run it before a long note, or before a note on a row near its limits. If TEXT does not fit, shorten it, or cut the notes with `rewrite` (below).
106	- `$L rewrite N FILE` replaces row N with the whole line in FILE, a file under your tree's `tmp/`, with N or `?` in its number cell. Use it to correct the claim, cut the notes or change the reproducer. The tool checks the line against the template and keeps the old line in the history file.
107	- `$L duplicate N --of M` makes row N a pointer to row M.
108	- `$L close N --commit HASH --test NAME` marks row N `FIXED`, by the commit HASH and its test NAME. Run it once that commit is in `HEAD`, and commit the close after it. NAME can also be a file under `explorations/coordinator/tools/`, or `none` with `--note REASON`. For a `CONTESTED` row, add `--settled TEXT`, which names what settled its question.
109	- `$L landing-check BASE` prints each problem, and exits 1 on any. Run it when your brief asks for it. It checks the whole ledger against the template, so a broken row that BASE already had counts too. The problems are a row that breaks the template, an `XXX` test deleted or renamed while a row that is not closed names it, a row that is not closed though a commit says it fixed it, and a FACTS or POSITIONS entry that disagrees with a row's status.
110	
111	## The repository's history
112	
113	- The repository is a 2018 fork of `sirinath/fortress`, a git conversion of the project's java.net Mercurial repository. Its trunk runs from 2007-01-04 to 2012-08-31 and ends at `a874948ac`, the team's last commit.
114	- The commits after `a874948ac` are the revival's. After the tag `sealed-tree`, commit `75cca6683`, the revival began to fix the team's code, test first. Before it, the revival changed mainly the build and the toolchain.
115	- `git diff a874948ac -- FILE` shows what the revival changed in a file, and `git diff 75cca6683 -- FILE` what it changed after the tag.
116	- If the commands above fail, run `git rev-parse --is-shallow-repository`. It prints `true` in a shallow clone, where these commits do not resolve. There, a copyright header of Sun Microsystems or Oracle, as in `Library/Format.fss`, marks a file that the team made, but not which of its lines the port or the revival changed. If your task needs those lines, say in your report that the clone is shallow.
117	- The conversion cut 146 parent links, so a `git log` of a directory stops at a cut and misses the team's earlier commits. Use `git log --follow` on a file, or compare contents.
118	- To find who wrote something, or where the repository's history after 2012 comes from, read `research/authorship.md` and `explorations/coordinator/lineage.md`.
119	- Commit `8fe1daa8f` copied a third-party port of the tree to Java 9 onto the team's last commit, `a874948ac`. Give its lines no credit, and name no author of it in any text that you commit. In a reconstruction of authorship, attribute nothing of it to anyone.

1	# Committing and pushing
2	
3	**scratch**
4	: Files and folders that your work makes and `main` does not keep: logs, captured and raw run output, copies of tools, probe programs, lists and private caches folders.
5	
6	Your brief says whether you commit and push, and on which branch. If it says nothing, commit on your current branch, and push it.
7	
8	## What to commit
9	
10	- Commit your change, its tests, your report if it is a file, and any reusable script.
11	- Commit what you write to the record, such as a ledger row, with the work that it records. A row's close follows the fix's commit (`records.md`).
12	- Keep scratch in your tree's `tmp/`, which is gitignored.
13	- In a fresh clone, `.claude/worktrees/` and `.claude/agents/` show as untracked, because the lines of `.git/info/exclude` that hide them are not in the clone. Do not commit them.
14	- Keep a copyrighted PDF or deck in `research/decks/`, which is gitignored. Cite it by its Wayback URL. Notes on it go in `research/extracts/`: your own summary, with brief attributed quotations.
15	- Put provenance and rationale in commit messages and reports, not in source comments.
16	- Name a model by its tier (Opus, Sonnet, Fable) in any text that you commit, commit messages included. Never write its model identifier, the API's name for the model, which starts with `claude-`.
17	
18	## How to commit
19	
20	Commit as you go, each commit in one command that names its paths:
21	
22	    git add -- <paths> && git commit -m "<message>" -- <paths>
23	
24	- The command commits only the paths that it names. Other agents may have uncommitted edits in your tree. Leave them alone.
25	- If you renamed a file with `git mv`, name its old path in `git commit` only, because `git add` refuses a path that no longer exists: `git add -- <new paths> && git commit -m "<message>" -- <new paths> <old paths>`.
26	- Never commit a copied directory, and never use `git add -A`.
27	- Before you commit more than a few hundred lines, stage them and read what you staged: `git add -- <paths> && git diff --cached --stat -- <paths>`.
28	- If the commit edits the original tree, say so in its message.
29	- End every commit message with this footer, exactly, whatever footer Claude Code suggests:
30	
31	      Co-Authored-By: Claude <noreply@anthropic.com>
32	      Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_01AmiXNpJxQ6TBwec4vJZHDB
33	
34	  If your brief gives another session line, use it. If a commit that is already made has a footer that names a model, by any name or identifier, leave the commit as it is. Such a footer is not a defect: do not check for it, report it or list it.
35	
36	## Pushing
37	
38	Push after every commit, so that a lost container loses nothing.
39	
40	- If you work on your own branch, push it: `git push -u origin <branch>` the first time, then `git push`. Your brief says how the branch reaches `main`.
41	- From a session in a cloud container, do not try to delete a branch on GitHub, or retry a refusal with another tool (the `cloud-container` skill, "Rules for every agent"). Removing a worktree does not delete its branch, which stays. Ask nobody in your report to delete a branch.
42	- If you work on `main`, other agents commit to it too. Push only your own commits:
43	  1. Run `git log origin/main..main`. Your commits are those whose hashes your own `git commit` printed.
44	  2. If it lists another agent's commit, run the command again shortly: that agent pushes right after it commits. If the commit stays, push nothing, and say so in your report.
45	  3. If it lists only your commits, push the three refs with this one command, and wait for it to end:
46	
47	         git push --atomic origin main main:claude/worker-brief-fable-vnnuv8 main:blinded-fable
48	
49	     With `--atomic`, the three refs update together or not at all. Do not pipe the command into another command, since a pipe hides a refusal. A refusal shows as a line that starts with `!`, and as a non-zero exit. The last ref keeps `blinded-fable` current. If the container is lost, the platform rebuilds it from that branch.
50	- Push no branch that this section does not name, unless your brief names it.
51	- If a push is refused, push nothing more, and do not run it again. Report the refused ref and git's message.
52

100	## Note 7. Chapter 1, Introduction: "The name “Fortress” is derived from the intent to produce a “secure Fortran”, i.e., …"
101	
102	https://palimondo.github.io/fortress/specification/intro.html#p-f9d62312
103	
104	The text says what the two words stand for, and gives no measure. The chapter's first sentence calls Fortress a language "for producing robust high-performance software with high programmability" (`Specification/preliminaries/intro/philosophy.tex:12-18`). So the claim is about the pair, speed with ease of writing, and not about speed alone.
105	
106	## Note 8. Chapter 1, section 1.1: "Although Fortress is statically and nominally typed, types are not specified for all fields, …"
107	
108	https://palimondo.github.io/fortress/specification/intro.html#p-284c2aab
109	
110	"Nominally typed" means that two types are the same type only if they have the same name. The inference of left-out parameter types was a wish: the team never wrote how it works, and only one case of it is built.
111	
112	**Nominal typing.**
113	A trait type is known by its name and its declared `extends` clause. Two traits with the same methods are still two types. Swift's protocols and Scala's traits work the same way. The opposite is structural typing, where a type is known by its shape. Fortress has both: trait types are nominal, and tuple types and function types are structural (`Specification/basic/types-vals-vars.tex:21-26`). So `(ZZ32, String)` needs no declaration.
114	
115	**What the specification says of left-out types.**
116	
117	- The introduction's sentence is the team's. Versions 1.0 alpha, 1.0 beta and 1.0 print it too.
118	- The Working Draft's chapter on type inference was a heading and two draft notes. The first note reads: "This chapter will include the Fortress static type inference mechanism." (`Specification-1.0-frozen/basic/inference.tex`; F-169).

\begin{figure}[p]
The Fortress Language Specification, Version 1.0\cite{Fortress} was the first to be
released in tandem with a compliant interpreter (as of March 31, 2008),
available as open source and online at:\\

\begin{center}
{\tt http://projectfortress.sun.com}\\[1em]
\end{center}
Our tandem release of a specification and matching interpreter was a major
milestone for the project.
Our reference implementation has been evolving gradually,
in parallel with the evolution of the language specification and
the development of the core libraries.  In order to synchronize
the specification with the implementation, it was necessary both to add
features to the implementation and to drop features from the specification.
All Fortress source code appearing in the specification has been
tested by executing it with the open source Fortress implementation. Moreover,
all code has been rendered automatically with the tool \emph{Fortify}, also
included with the standard Fortress distribution. Fortify is an open source tool
for converting Fortress source code to \LaTeX.\\


Since the release, we have incrementally added back
features taken out of the specification as they have been implemented.
In particular, we have been building a Fortress compiler with a static
type checker and various static constraints checker.
We also made considerable amount of modification and evolution of the
language design.\\


This specification is a working draft;
it is meant to include all language features included in
the Fortress Language Specification, Version 1.0\EXP{\beta{}}
(perhaps with additional ) and any language changes since then.
This version of the specification is not yet for a release;
it may include wild ideas that require additional research before they can be
implemented reliably.
This specification includes descriptions of unimplemented features in boxes
at the beginning of sections,
and informal comments and notes in boxes in the margin.
\end{figure}


\begin{figure}[p]
The not-yet-supported features include:
\begin{itemize}
\item widening coercion
\item multifix operators
\item type coverage check
\item generic overloading check
\item definite assignment check
\item keyword and varargs parameters
\item varargs expressions
\item some modifiers (\KWD{override}, \KWD{io}, \KWD{atomic}, \KWD{value}, ...)
\item qualified names
\item identifiers including connecting punctuations
\item ASCII conversion
\item Unicode canonicalization
\item array comprehensions
\item reduction variables
\item object copy
\item unboxed types
\item mutual recursion in value objects
\item thread fairness guarantee
\item distributions
\item matrix unpasting
\item Non-type static parameters
\item dimensions and units
\item tests and properties
\item type aliases
\item where clauses and conditional extension
\item abstract function declarations
\item checked exceptions, deferred exceptions, and chained exceptions
\item contract checking (overloaded functionals and method overriding)
\item static expressions, static range types, and some range operations
\item some types (\TYP{HeapSequence},
\TYP{LinearSequence}, $\mathbb{Q}$,
\TYP{Numeral}, \EXP{\mathbb{Z}}, \EXP{\mathbb{N}}, \EXP{\mathbb{Q}}, ...)
\item some operators on aggregate expressions
\item some functions in \secref{other-expressions}
\item tail-call optimization
\item compound APIs check
\item import API names
\item components linking
\end{itemize}

<!-- Answers to the curator's notes 3 to 15 of `notes-export-2026-11-15.txt`, written on the preface, chapter 1 and chapter 2 of the specification's HTML reader: what the preface's list of features not yet supported holds today on each path, what "nominally typed" and the inference of left-out types mean and do, a primer on multiple dispatch, the "resident fortress" and today's commands, where `run`'s `args` went, and file names against component names; with the faults found in the specification's text. -->

# Answers to the notes of 2026-11-15

Every program below ran on 2026-11-15, at commit `d9918f9098`, from a scratch folder with a private caches folder.
The two ways to run a program have these names here:

- **walk**: the interpreter. `fortress P.fss` and `fortress walk P.fss` are the same command.
- **compiled path**: `fortress compile P.fss` writes JVM bytecode, and `fortress run P` runs it.

A **row** is a row of the gap ledger, `explorations/fortress-gap-ledger.md`.
**P-N** is a decision in `explorations/coordinator/POSITIONS.md`.
**F-N** is a fact in `explorations/coordinator/FACTS.md`.
The **Working Draft** is the team's unrevised text of February 2011, in `Specification-1.0-frozen/`.

## Note 3. About this working draft: "widening coercion"

https://palimondo.github.io/fortress/specification/preface.html#p-f85a28b6

Yes. Widening coercion is built on both paths today.

- Each wider number type declares a `coerce` from each narrower one. A value converts at a call, at a typed binding and at an assignment (P-74).
- The compiled path chooses the coercion by the static type. Walk has no static types, so it chooses by the value at run time (P-59).
- Two cases still fail under walk. A body with a declared return type is not converted (row 387). The elements of a tuple are not converted (row 395).

## Note 4. About this working draft: "some modifiers (override, io, atomic, value, ...)"

https://palimondo.github.io/fortress/specification/preface.html#p-0ee6a8b8

Yes for `atomic` and `value`, with limits on the compiled path. `io` runs and nothing checks it. `override` works under walk only.

- `atomic` as a block, `atomic do ... end`, runs on both paths. As a function's modifier it runs under walk: a program with `atomic bump(): () = n += 1` printed `100` after 100 calls. The code generator refuses that modifier: "Don't know how to compile this kind of FnDecl" (row 304 holds the local function; row 650 holds the same refusal for `override`). `atomic` as an expression, without `do`, does not compile either (`references/compiler.md`, "What the compiled path cannot compile yet").
- `value` works on both paths. Two value objects of one type are equivalent when their fields are (P-168; row 906, fixed). Walk still lets a value object declare a `var` field (row 112). On the compiled path the modifier does not unbox the fields.
- `io` is accepted on both paths. A program with `io say(s: String): () = println s` printed its line under walk and compiled. Neither path checks what the modifier promises.
- `override`: walk checks at load that the declaration overrides something. The compiled checker accepts an `override` that overrides nothing (row 653). The code generator refuses every `override` (row 650).

## Note 5. About this working draft: "Non-type static parameters"

https://palimondo.github.io/fortress/specification/preface.html#p-56c0c623

Yes, `nat` is one of them, and it is built. A static parameter that is not a type has one of six kinds: `nat`, `int`, `bool`, `dim`, `unit` and `opr`.

- `nat` and `int` (sizes): built on both paths. The checker computes arithmetic on numerals and compares other sizes by their written form (P-55). Two open defects: a size of 2^31 or more read as a value (row 962), and a compiled call whose `where` clause introduces a size (row 867).
- `bool`: not usable. The compiled checker refuses to infer one (row 307). Walk stops at load on a method whose parameter type has one (row 761).

POSITIONS.md:57
- P-59 **Walk chooses a coercion by the run-time value until it runs the checker, after the switch-over.** Walk has no static types. So where a coercion is needed, walk chooses it by the value's run-time type. The specification and the compiled path choose it by the static type. The curator accepts this as the interpreter's limit, and walk is not changed for it before the switch-over. A callout in the coercion chapter (`Specification/basic/conversions-coercions.tex`) states the limit. Two expected-failure tests record it: `XXXCoercionStaticRungC`, the chapter's own printed example, and `XXXCoercionStaticNarrowRungC`. After the switch-over, once walk runs the checker on its programs (P-12 orders the two steps), it uses the static coercions that the checker inserts.

POSITIONS.md:61
- P-147 **An object defines an inherited abstract method when its bodies of that name at narrower parameter types together cover the abstract method's parameter types.** That is, each value of the abstract method's parameter types is a value of one body's parameter types. A `comprises` clause counts as the compiled checker reads it, which is P-60's reading: a closed trait is covered by its listed types. A body at the abstract method's own parameter types is the plain case. This is the team's rule of 2012, in Steele's abstract-method check of the compiled checker and in the Covered rule of the Welterweight calculus (`Papers/Welterweight/`). So the team's `Library/Pairs.fss` and `ProjectFortress/tests/FileConversion.fss` stay valid: an object in each defines an inherited abstract operator once for each type that a `comprises` clause lists. Walk applies the same rule at load, and its earlier allowance of any one narrower body goes. The traits chapter's sentence, which admitted no narrower body, is revised in the specification's revision form (P-96). Row 725: the acceptance of some valid objects whose methods have static parameters of their own, which the checker and walk (row 728) refuse. Row 665: walk's check of generic objects, which its load check skips.

POSITIONS.md:58
- P-60 **The specification reads a `comprises` clause at the level of values.** `trait S comprises { U, V }` says that every value of `S` is a value of `U` or of `V`. So another trait may stand between `S` and its listed types. The specification defines "covers" once: a type covers another when every value of the second is a value of the first. The Meet Rule gains a case for closed traits. Where the rule asks for a declaration at the meet of two overloads' parameter types, several declarations below both serve, if together they cover the meet. So a call whose argument's static type stands between closed traits and their listed types may have several most specific declarations. The call's type is the intersection of their return types, and the declaration that runs is unique only at run time. The compiled checker uses coverage only in its overloading rules, to accept an overload set and to justify a call's tie among several most specific declarations, and not in its general subtype test. Why: the proof addendum (`reviews/comprises-type-level-proof-addendum.md`) shows this sound for ground declarations, at calls that need no coercion. A ground declaration's types hold no type variable, and `G[\ZZ32\]` is ground. The addendum shows it for coverage used only in that way, and leaves any wider use to a review of its own. A call that needs a coercion is outside the proof too (F-76 gives what the compiled checker does there). A declaration with static parameters, whose instance dispatch must choose at run time, is outside the proof: one instance would have to meet every one of the return types at once. The typing by the intersection is not extended to it, and the specification states that boundary. Rows 543 and 551: the compiled checker gives no call an intersection type where any declaration of the family has static parameters, and walk checks no `comprises` clause declared outside the main component.

POSITIONS.md:43
- P-45 **Overloaded declarations may differ in their static parameters.** The specification drops its sentence that forbids this, and keeps it as superseded text. It states instead the overloading model of the type group's 2011 paper (`Papers/Types/`), which the compiled checker already used. The checker keeps the paper's three rules: No Duplicates, Meet and Return Type. It checks the Return Type Rule over every instance of a generic declaration that the argument types allow, not over one guessed instance. One rule of the old sentence survives: if one generic declaration is more specific than another, their static parameters must line up position by position, as Java's rule for overriding a generic method requires. The compiled checker tests it only where the two declarations have as many static parameters of their own (F-75). Walk chooses among overloads by the parameter types that each declaration declares, not by the order in which they are written. At load, walk judges each pair of two generic declarations by the checker's rules on their declared parameter types. It does not refuse a pair only because none of their parameter types exclude, as when one declaration is more specific than the other. Walk and the checker must accept the same pairs. The library repairs, by declarations of its own, the overload sets that the checker refused, and no line of microGPT's two programs changes. Where walk or the checker still judges a pair against these rules: walk compares two functional methods of a generic trait or object on the instance that a call makes (F-26); both paths refuse the paper's own valid example (row 539); walk refuses two generic functional methods of a trait without static parameters whose declared domains lie one inside the other, and fails at a call on such a pair in a generic trait (rows 779 and 780); and walk and the checker disagree on three kinds of pair (rows 786 to 788).

POSITIONS.md:65
- P-152 **Walk and the compiled checker read the exclusion of two generic declarations over their whole parameter types, by existential reduction.** With static parameters, the parameter types of two declarations can exclude each other as a whole, even where no single parameter excludes its counterpart. In `o[\T\](x: P[\T\], b: Box[\T\])` beside `o[\T\](x: Q[\T\], b: Box[\T\])`, where `P[\T\]` excludes `Q[\T\]` only at the same `T`, neither parameter excludes alone. But no value is a `Box` of two types, so `b` fixes the same `T` for both declarations, and no argument fits both. A generic trait in `Box`'s place fixes `T` in the same way. Both paths read such a pair as excluding, and judge it on that reading by the overloading rules (P-45: the 2011 paper's No Duplicates, Meet and Return Type rules). Why: the type group's 2011 paper decides exclusion between parameter types with static parameters by existential reduction (`Papers/Types/exc-reduction.tick`), as the revised specification states (`Specification/advanced/overloading.tex`, "Declarations with Static Parameters"). Walk refuses such a pair at load where one declaration has a `where` clause, which the checker accepts (row 787); and walk reads an object type over a static parameter, such as `Box[\T\]`, as excluding a type that it equals at some instance, such as `Box[\ZZ32\]`, so that it loads a pair that the checker refuses (row 788).

POSITIONS.md:64
- P-151 **Only the `where`-clause forms that the team wrote down are built: conditional extension, a function's or a method's condition, and `AnyList`'s `comprises` clause.** A `where` clause states conditions on static parameters, and may introduce static variables of its own, as `where [\E\]` does. A trait or object that extends a type under a `where` condition is that type only where the condition holds, and its members are checked with the condition holding (conditional extension). A `where` condition on a function's or a method's own static parameters bounds them. The team's commented-out clause `AnyList comprises List[\E\] where [\E\]` becomes live, which clears the type error of `AnyList`'s join `||`; its other operations, `addLeft` and `addRight`, move into `List` (row 799). `SUM`'s fusion with `MAX` and `MIN`, the library's fast path for the maximum or the minimum of sums, stays. A method's `where` condition clears four of the fusion's six type errors; for the other two, the team's commented-out generic `distribute` is the fix measured (F-242 holds the measurement: as the team wrote it, it only moves them). Why: a feature with little support in the team's work bends the language beyond what the curator can review. He has such a feature built where the team left enough design intent for it, or where it is on the critical path to running fast compiled. Row 773: the members scoped to the condition, since a member checked under it stays callable where the condition fails. Row 774: walk's half of conditional extension. F-181 holds the code generator's half.

POSITIONS.md:104
- P-173 **A numeral converts where it stands: where its place fixes a type, into that type at compile time from its exact value; where nothing fixes one, into the machine default, a `ZZ32`, or a `ZZ64` or `ZZ` when its value does not fit, and with a radix point an `RR64`.** A place fixes a type when its declared type has a coercion from the numeral type, as the eight number types have and a program's own type may (P-174); `Any`, `Object`, `Number`, an unbounded type parameter and no declared type take the default. So `x = 3` is a `ZZ32`, and `x SEQV z` is `true` for `z: ZZ32 = 3`; `bigN = 3000000000` is a `ZZ64` at its binding (row 946). The default applies to a numeral, a literal after the fold, never to an expression of a numeral type, and a `nat` parameter used as a value is a `ZZ32` where it is a size (P-40), and a `ZZ` where it is one of a numeral type's four numbers (P-174). A type parameter that several numerals fix takes the narrowest default that holds every value, an `RR64` where any has a radix point, each numeral converting into it exactly; a float numeral whose conversions into `QQ` and `RR64` tie reads `RR64`. At a typed place the conversion is exact or rounds once (P-76, P-172), and a numeral outside the type's range is refused statically; walk converts from the exact value at the same places, place by place, before it runs the checker (P-12). An expression of numerals alone folds exactly before the checker into a signed constant, which defaults as an integer numeral, as a `QQ` for a quotient, or as an `RR64` with a radix point: so `x = 7/2` is a `QQ`, `1/2 = 0.5` is `true`, and `-2147483648`, prefix minus on a numeral, folded, is a `ZZ32`. `gg(5, w)`, with `gg` declared at `(ZZ32, T)` and at `(Any, Any)`, runs the `ZZ32` declaration (P-49). The parameter types of the declaration that a call runs are places that fix a type, and a numeral argument goes to the most specific declaration that takes it, by its own conversion if need be, with its default as the last resort: `u = 0` is `true` for `u: NN32 = 0`, the numeral an `NN32` at `NN32`'s own `=` (P-46 gives the rule and its ground; row 1016 holds where walk departs, and row 1017 where both paths do). Why: the design completes the Working Draft's, whose numerals have types of their own so that a library decides by coercions how they meet other types (P-174 gives that ground). It bends P-26 in t

POSITIONS.md:102
- P-171 **Two string literals of one text are one object, on both paths, and a concatenation of two string literals is folded into one literal.** P-168's rule stands: strings are reference objects, and their text equality is their own `=`. So `"ab" SEQV "ab"` is `true`, also for one literal evaluated twice, and so is `("foo" || "bar") SEQV "foobar"`, by the fold that `Specification/basic/expressions/constant.tex:129-133` names; a string built at run time is not `SEQV` an equal literal, unless Java answers the same object, as `substring(0, length)` answers the string itself, and then both paths answer `true`. Walk interns each literal's text with `String.intern()` as its evaluator makes the string, and its `SEQV` compares two flat strings' carried Java strings by `==`. The compiled path keeps loading each literal with `ldc`, which yields the JVM's interned `String` (JVM specification, 5.1), and `equality.sEquiv` compares the Java strings that two `FJavaString` wrappers carry by `==`, not the wrappers. The specification gains, in the revision form (P-96), a sentence that a string literal denotes one object and one on the folded concatenation. The team's test `compiler_regressions/seqv.fss:22`, `"cat"==="cat"`, passes on the one library as written. Why: every team source that speaks of literals makes equal literals one value: the specification's "Literals are values; they do not require evaluation" (`literals.tex:25-26`), the 2012 restart's "All literals represent value objects" (`Documentation/Specification/Prose/Language/Expressions/literals.tick:29`), the team's code of 2008 and 2010, and that test; and Java, Kotlin, Scala and Clojure, whose strings are Java strings, give equal literals one object. Detail: `reviews/literals-2026-11-08.md`, sections 6.1 and 6.4, way S-b with its compiled way (i), and way S-d.

POSITIONS.md:53
- P-55 **A size may hold arithmetic, compared by its written form once its numerals are computed.** The compiled checker accepts a sum, a difference, a product or a power as a size, such as the length in `Vector[\RR64, 16\]`. It computes each operation whose operands are both numerals, from the inside out, so `2 3` is the size `6`. Otherwise it compares two sizes by their written form: `s0 s1` is not the same size as `s1 s0`, though their values are equal. On the compiled path, the class loader computes a size's value when it makes the class of an instantiation. Walk already computes such a size exactly when it makes an instance. The checker counts a size name, such as `b0`, as possibly equal to a numeral, as the team's Q&A in `Specification/appendices/internal-document.tex` answers. So the `N[\0\]` arm of a `typecase N[\b0\]` is reachable. The library keeps the team's sizes written as products and sums, such as a matrix's storage of `s0 s1` cells. F-146 states what the checker accepts.

== explorations/coordinator/FACTS.md, ## Execution model

FACTS.md:16
- F-22 **When a component's name differs from the api that it exports, neither path finds the component, for an exported function or variable alike.** The specification resolves an imported api to any component that exports it (`Specification/basic/components/overview.tex`). The tree looks only under the api's name, unless a user maps the api to its component by hand with `LinkShell`'s `alink` or `clink`. The linker's component repository looks this way (`Linker.whoIsImplementingMyAPI`), so `fortress link` and walk print "Could not find an implementation for API … on path" before any code is generated. The code generator names a reference to an exported declaration after the api, and the declaring class after the component. The link step rewrites such a reference to the component only when the repository names it, so files compiled one by one, without `fortress link`, die with `NoClassDefFoundError`. The missing step is the repository's: finding the component that exports the api. The report names two repairs, neither built: the repository could search the source path for that component, or the code generator could emit api-named forwarders, for which three comments in `CodeGen.java` leave a place. Walk and `fortress link` need the first. Workaround: name the api after its component. Gated by the expected failure `compiler_tests/XXXExportVarRungXLinked.test` (row 320). Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-export-var/REPORT.md`, "The measurement that separates them".

A trait's or object's contract does not reach the refusal: the disambiguator drops it (row 781); F-255 says how each path reads a `where` clause on an `extends` entry (row 774). Where a generic type that such a clause lists gives a member's body, the code generator crashes first (row 812). A function's or method's own clause that introduces a `where`-clause variable compiles, and the compiled call dies with `NoClassDefFoundError` (row 867). Tests: `compiler_tests/WhereBoundFunctionCompiled`, `WhereBoundMethodCompiled`, `WhereBoundObjectCompiled`, `WhereBoundTraitMethodCompiled`, `ComprisesWhereFunctionalMethodCompiled`; `XXXFunctionContractCodeGeneration`; the `XXXNatOpenRun` pair; the `XXXWhereVariableCallCompiled` pair. | 29 | multifix dispatch is absent: walk never looks for an *n*-argument definition of an infix operator repeated between three or more operands, and reassociates to binary calls | NEGATIVE-VERIFIED | implementation gap (walk) | `Specification/basic/operators/chained-multifix.tex`, "Chained and Multifix Operators"; `Specification-1.0-frozen/fortress/preamble.tex:59` (multifix among the not-yet-supported features) | none | ours | Walk applies an operator of more than two operands pairwise, left to right, unless it is enclosing (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/interpreter/evaluator/Evaluator.java:994`). `a OTIMES b OTIMES c = V(24.0, n=2)`: the right value with two children, so two binary calls (probe `explorations/spec-probes/p13_multifix2.fss`, in the parent of e879b6a44). A tight juxtaposition of three non-function items with a ternary `opr juxtaposition` declared runs the binary ones too: `a(b)(c)` gives `123` where the compiled path's multifix gives `1023`, for `K(10 a.i + b.i)` and `K(900 + 100 a.i + 10 b.i + c.i)` (at a1a75716a). Workaround: a reduction over a concatenation monoid. |

The check runs only where the object's type is no instance of a generic: `declared = !(selfType instanceof GenericTypeInstance)` (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/interpreter/evaluator/values/Constructor.java:263` at cdb84fba5), and `checkForDef` returns for an instance (`:431`); the check reads no generic declaration. `XXXAbstractMethodUndefinedGenericObjectExpressionWalk` gates the object expression. The `override` check reads generic types at the declaration (`BuildEnvironments.java:895`). A check of each instance would ask for coverage (P-147), which by reading `IntMap`'s and `Random`'s objects now meet (rows 667, 668); not measured at instances. |

Gathered by reading git and the files, with no build and no run. -->

# Who built what on the preface's list

## The answer

The curator is right. The list is not the state of February 2011, and most of what works today on it is the team's.

- The team wrote the list on 2009-11-09 and last changed its items on 2009-11-11. The commit of 2011-02-02 changed only the copyright header. The team never touched the list again, up to its last commit in 2012.
- Of the 27 named items, 16 work today, whole or in part, as Note 6 states them. The other 11 do not work at all, so they have no part to attribute.
- Of the 16: the team wrote the working part of 8. The team and the revival each wrote some of the working part of 7. The revival wrote the working part of 1 (where clauses and conditional extension).
- No item is unsettled as a whole. Two points inside items need a run of the team's tree: whether a compiled multifix chain ran, and whether walk's check of abstract methods stopped a program.
- So the sentence "how far the revival has come on the team's own to-do list" does not hold. Half of the working items were the team's alone, and for 6 of the 7 shared ones the team's part was in the tree at the draft's date.

How an item is sorted here: by who wrote the code or the library lines that carry the part that works today. "The team" means the tree at `a874948ac`. "The revival" means the commits after `8fe1daa8f` (2026-08-18). Nothing of `8fe1daa8f` itself is counted for anyone. All findings are by reading. No program ran.

## What the preface says the list is

The file is `Specification-1.0-frozen/fortress/preamble.tex`. It equals `Specification/fortress/preamble.tex` at `a874948ac`, byte for byte.

- The first paragraph speaks of the interpreter: version 1.0 was "released in tandem with a compliant interpreter (as of March 31, 2008)" (`:13-14`).
- The second paragraph speaks of the compiler: "we have been building a Fortress compiler with a static type checker and various static constraints checker" (`:35-37`).
- The list has one line of introduction: "The not-yet-supported features include:" (`:56`). It names no implementation and no date.
- The draft "includes descriptions of unimplemented features in boxes at the beginning of sections" (`:49-51`). Those boxes repeat the list's items, chapter by chapter.

The file's versions in the team's history, found by reading the file at each of the team's 5,397 commits (a `git log` of the path stops at a cut of the conversion, at `5a68404fdf`):

- `5da7257089`, 2009-10-20: the preamble, without the list.
- `61e28a78c4`, 2009-11-09, "[spec] Added a list of NYI features.": the list, with every item of today.
- `93f5018fd2`, 2009-11-11: three items reworded ("where clauses" gains "and conditional extension", "contract checking" gains its parenthesis, "some types" gains `Numeral`, ℤ, ℕ, ℚ), and one spelling.
- `2f8b4331a`, 2011-02-02, "Updated Copyright notices": the header only. This version stays to `a874948ac`: 971 commits hold it.

The revival changed two items of the list in `Specification/`, in `4978a9b16e` (2026-11-09): "static expressions" gained "beyond the folding of numerals and of string literals", and "some types" lost `Numeral`.

## The 16 items that work today, whole or in part

### The team wrote the working part (8)

**Multifix operators.** The compiled checker's case for a repeated operator tries the multifix declaration first, then the binary ones. It is the same six lines at `2f8b4331a` and at `a874948ac` (`scala_src/typechecker/impls/Operators.scala:376-381`). The revival's `054c4bcfd9` (2026-10-09) passes the expected type into that case and changes nothing else of it (F-221). Not settled by reading: whether the team's code generator ran such a chain. The team's only test that names multifix, `compiler_tests/XXX5aw.test`, checks error messages. A compile and run, at `a874948ac`, of a program with a ternary `opr OPLUS` would settle it. Walk makes binary calls in the team's tree and today (row 29).

**Identifiers including connecting punctuation.** The team's library binds names with an underscore at the draft's date: `o_n : ZZ32 = o - b0` (`Library/FortressLibrary.fss:2167` at `2f8b4331a`). No commit of the revival is on this. The limit on `W_1` (row 15) is the team's lexer too.

**ASCII conversion.** The part that Note 6 calls built, the conversion of names, is the team's. The appendix's draft note, "Only [the section on names] is supported", is in the frozen text (`Specification-1.0-frozen/appendices/ascii-to-unicode.tex:15`). One thing changed after Note 6 was written: `5c8055dee` (2026-11-16) makes `∑` and `∏` begin a reduction, and row 5 is closed. That is the revival's, and it is outside the conversion of names.

**Tests and properties.** The `test` command is in `Shell.java` at both dates (`:439` at `2f8b4331a`, `:473` at `a874948ac`), and calls `walkTests`. The team's library declares `test` functions at the draft's date (`Library/Avl.fss`, `Relation.fss`, `SetClosure.fss`, `String.fss`, `ChunkedSparseArray.fss`). No commit of the revival changed the command. The frozen chapter's own note speaks of "the limited form the interpreter supports" (row 120).

**Abstract function declarations.** In a trait, the team's tests declare abstract methods on both paths at the draft's date: 10 files of `compiler_tests/` and 5 of `tests/` and `Library/` hold an `abstract` method line at `2f8b4331a`. The revival added one case to the checker, a type's abstract functional methods (`c23b85fdc2`, 2026-10-16). At top level the declarations run on neither path, then and now.

**Contract checking.** Walk's `requires` and `ensures` are the team's: `tests/contracts1.fss` dates from 2008-02-09 (`f7feee2e7e`, "Requires"), and `interpreter/rewrite/DesugarerVisitor.java` holds `CallerViolation` at both dates. No commit of the revival is on walk's contracts. The code generator's refusal (row 701) is the state the team left.

**Some types.** `trait ZZ` and `trait QQ` are in walk's library at the draft's date (`Library/FortressLibrary.fss:822` and `:521` at `2f8b4331a`), and already on 2009-11-09 (`61e28a78c4`), two days before the list gained ℤ and ℚ. The compiler's library has no `ZZ` at `2f8b4331a` and has one at `a874948ac` (`ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/CompilerBuiltin.fsi:102`), so that one is the team's work after the draft. The revival reshaped walk's number types into siblings (`d846e3644c`, 2026-09-27) and made `ZZ`'s and `QQ`'s values value objects (`598331c0d`, 2026-11-07). It added no type of this item.

**Components linking.** `fortress link` as it works today is the team's, and later than the draft. `linker/Linker.java` first appears on 2012-01-31 (`1d4e967aac`). At `2f8b4331a` the folder `linker/` does not exist, though `Shell.java:376` already has a `link` command. The revival's one commit on this is `4e4b80253` (2026-09-20), which lets a mutable variable cross an api (row 320, the fixed half). The revival has no commit on `Linker.java`.

### The team and the revival each wrote some of it (7)

**Widening coercion.** The compiled path's coercion is the team's, from before the list: `scala_src/typechecker/CoercionOracle.scala` dates from 2009-04-02 (`ab00f28ad2`), and `compiler_tests/Compiled9.CompiledCoercions.fss` from 2009-10-02 (`67e2222f56`, "Added lifting of coercion declarations and definitions"). The compiler's library declares 6 `coerce` at `2f8b4331a` (`ZZ32` into `ZZ64`, `RR32` into `RR64`, and from literals) and 15 at `a874948ac`. Walk's half is the revival's. Walk's library declares no `coerce` at `a874948ac` and 23 today, the first in `d846e3644c` (2026-09-27). The team's walk left it as a note: "TODO add checks for COERCE, right here" (`interpreter/evaluator/values/OverloadedFunction.java:792` at `a874948ac`). Walk converts since `b628871a26` (2026-09-26) and `0416821881` (2026-09-29). The `widens` declaration itself is in no library at any of the three commits (P-74 defers it).

**Type coverage check.** As Note 6 reads it. The compiled check is the team's: `scala_src/typechecker/AbstractMethodChecker.scala` dates from 2009-08-13 (`d2ed6ba762`), is 210 lines at the draft's date, and was reworked in 2012 (185 lines at `a874948ac`). The team's tests `compiler_tests/XXX6an.test` and `XXX6m.test` expect its message. Walk's `checkForDef` is in `Constructor.java` at both dates. The revival added the reading of coverage through a `comprises` clause on both paths (`59b1d0a4d2` and `f9fe5c8742`, 2026-10-14) and walk's refusal at load (`fdd377ead9`, 2026-10-09). Not settled by reading: whether the team's walk stopped a program by `checkForDef`. A run at `a874948ac` of an object that leaves an inherited abstract method without a body would settle it. The draft's only other use of the word is "the coverage check" of the Meet Rule (`Specification-1.0-frozen/appendices/future.tex:285`). On that reading the item is the revival's (P-60; `e2f1aa7e8b`, 2026-09-30, "accepts the Meet Rule's comprises example").

**Generic overloading check.** The compiled checker's check is the team's: `OverloadingChecker.scala` dates from 2009-03-07 (`9f196847ad`), and at the draft's date it reads static parameters in its exclusion and meet tests (`:351-402`). The team reworked it by 2012 to the model of its 2011 paper, which P-45 says the checker "already used". The revival added the Return Type Rule over every instance (`e2f1aa7e8b`, 2026-09-30), the Meet Rule for functional methods (`70d5486f99`), exclusion by existential reduction (P-152; `64fa505c4e`), and all of walk's load check of generic pairs (`8f7e183d49`, `6d187d0697`).

**Keyword and varargs parameters.** Walk's varargs are the team's, from the start: `tests/restTest.fss` is in the first commit (2007-01-04), and the library uses them at the draft's date (`assert(x:Any, y:Any, failMsg: Any...)`, `Library/FortressLibrary.fss:296`). The team's `tests/XXXvarargsObject.fss` records the constructor's limit (row 11). The compiled checker's typing of a varargs parameter is the revival's (`aa07efb310`, 2026-10-03; F-86). Keyword parameters: neither.

**Some modifiers.** The team's: the `atomic` block on both paths (9 files of `compiler_tests/` use it at `2f8b4331a`); walk's reading of `value` (`FTraitOrObject.java:98`) and of `override` (`Constructor.java:459`), both at the draft's date; the parser's acceptance of `io` and of `atomic` on a function. The revival's: `SEQV` on value objects on the compiled path (`598331c0d`, 2026-11-07; row 906), and walk's refusal of an `override` that overrides nothing (`fdd377ead9`, 2026-10-09). One correction to Note 4: no code reads the `atomic` modifier of a function. `Modifiers.isAtomic()` has no caller at `2f8b4331a`, at `a874948ac` or today. So "it runs under walk" means that walk accepts the modifier and ignores it, as the team's walk did.

**Non-type static parameters.** Walk's `nat` and `opr` parameters are the team's: `trait Rank[\ nat n \]` (`Library/FortressLibrary.fss:1592`) and `tests/oprTests.fss`, at both dates. The compiler's library also has `nat` parameters at the draft's date (`LibraryBuiltin/NativeArray.fss`, `NatReflect.fss`). The compiled checker's check of `nat` and `int` is the revival's (`3f297441c3`, 2026-09-26; P-55).

**Static expressions.** The fold of numerals and of string literals is the revival's (`3de571bac7` and `4978a9b16e`, 2026-11-09; P-173, P-171). Arithmetic in a size under walk is the team's: `PrimitiveArray[\T, (s0 s1) \]` at `Library/FortressLibrary.fss:2416` at `2f8b4331a`. The compiled checker's reading of such a size is the revival's (`3f297441c3`; P-55).

### The revival wrote the working part (1)

**Where clauses and conditional extension.** The team's tree parses the clauses and does no more. Its test says so: `tests/conditionalExtension.fss` at `2f8b4331a` ends `println "Conditional extension with where clauses can be parsed."`, and by `a874948ac` a copy is also in `not_passing_yet/`. The team's library keeps its clauses in comments: `(* comprises List[\E\] where [\E\] *)` (`Library/List.fss:87` at `a874948ac`), "not yet" (`Library/FortressLibrary.fsi:814`, `:1059`). The checker of `a874948ac` passes a `where` clause into its type analyzer (`STypeChecker.scala:184-202`), with "To Do: Check for the where-clause variables" (`TypeWellFormedChecker.scala:54`). The three forms of P-151 are the revival's: `2b1cd8e639` and `24db899faa` (2026-10-17), `396e4ed8da` (2026-10-18), and the code generator's `c324b841c9` (2026-10-31).

## The 11 items with nothing that works

Note 6 states these as built on neither path, so there is nothing to attribute: the definite assignment check; qualified names; array comprehensions; reduction variables; distributions; matrix unpasting; dimensions and units; type aliases; checked, deferred and chained exceptions; tail-call optimization; import of api names.

## Not settled by reading

- Multifix: whether the team's compiled path ran a chain through a multifix declaration. The run is named above.
- Type coverage: whether the team's walk stopped at `checkForDef`. The run is named above.
- The group of nine small items of Note 6's last line was outside this note.
